items.q: The science of reciting the Qur'an correctly, giving each letter its due.
The word "tajwid" comes from a root meaning this.
Seeking refuge with Allah from Shaytan before reciting is called this.
Saying "Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim" is called this.
A pause or stop while reciting is called this.
Lengthening a vowel sound is called this.
The nasal sound made through the nose is called this.
A bouncing echo on certain letters when they carry sukun.
The number of qalqalah letters.
The phrase that gathers the qalqalah letters.
The vowel mark that means a letter has no vowel.
The mark that doubles a letter.
The two letters that always carry ghunnah when they have shaddah.
The place in the mouth or throat where a letter's sound comes from.
A teacher who passes on recitation with a connected chain gives this certificate.
The verse of Surah al-Muzzammil that commands measured recitation.
The heavy (full-mouthed) way of pronouncing a letter.
The light way of pronouncing a letter.
The natural lengthening of two counts.
The three letters of madd.
The vowel mark written above a letter for an "a" sound.
The vowel mark written below a letter for an "i" sound.
The vowel mark for a "u" sound.
The doubled vowel at the end of a noun, sounding like "-an, -in, -un" (meaning).
A nun with no vowel is called this.
A mim with no vowel is called this.
The length of ghunnah in counts.
The counting unit for madd, about the time to fold or open a finger.
The Arabic alphabet has this many letters.
The letters pronounced from the throat are called this.
The letters pronounced from the lips are called this.
The three lip letters.
The mark in the Mushaf meaning "it is better to stop here".
The mark in the Mushaf meaning "it is better to continue".
The mark in the Mushaf meaning "do not stop here".
The mark "mim" in the Mushaf means stopping here is this.
The mark "jim" in the Mushaf means stopping here is this.
Three dots appearing twice mean you may stop at one of them, not both; this is called this.
The small circle above a letter shows this.
Reciting slowly and calmly is called this, the slowest pace.
Reciting at a moderate pace is called this.
Reciting quickly while keeping the rules is called this.
Reciting from memory to a teacher is called this.
Listening to the teacher first, then repeating, is called this.
Our Beloved Master ﷺ said the one skilled in the Qur'an is with the noble righteous scribes (paraphrased).
Reading the Qur'an in a beautiful voice is called this.
Our Beloved Prophet ﷺ said: "Beautify the Qur'an with" this (paraphrased).
Mistakes in recitation are called this.
A clear mistake that changes the vowel or meaning.
A hidden mistake against the finer rules of tajwid.
Learning tajwid in practice is fard 'ayn on the reciter, says Ibn al-Jazari رحمة الله عليه; learning its theory is this.

items.q: The letter hamzah comes from this part of the throat.
The four rules of nun sakinah and tanwin.
The rule of pronouncing nun sakinah clearly, before the throat letters.
The number of throat letters for izhar.
The rule that turns nun sakinah into a mim sound before ba'.
The one letter that causes iqlab.
The rule that merges nun sakinah into the next letter.
The word that gathers the six letters of idgham.
The idgham letters that keep a ghunnah.
The two idgham letters that merge with no ghunnah.
The rule of hiding nun sakinah with ghunnah before 15 letters.
The number of letters of ikhfa' haqiqi.
The rule of mim sakinah before ba'.
The rule of mim sakinah before another mim.
The rule of mim sakinah before all other letters.
The well-known poem on tajwid for beginners by al-Jamzuri رحمة الله عليه.
The famous tajwid poem by Ibn al-Jazari رحمة الله عليه.
The lam of "Allah" is read heavy after these two vowels.
The lam of "Allah" is read light after this vowel.
The lam of "al-" that is pronounced before "moon letters".
The lam of "al-" that merges into "sun letters".
The six throat letters.
The two throat letters from the middle of the throat.
The two throat letters from the nearest part of the throat.
The letters of qalqalah.
Qalqalah is strongest when the letter has shaddah at a stop; this is called this.
Qalqalah in the middle of a word is called this.
Qalqalah at the end when stopping is called this.
The sun letters number this many.
The moon letters number this many.
The phrase that gathers the moon letters.
"Al-shams" is an example of this kind of lam.
"Al-qamar" is an example of this kind of lam.
The example of iqlab in "min ba'di".

items.q: "Man ya'mal" is an example of this rule.
"Min rabbihim" is an example of this rule.
"Min 'ilm" is an example of this rule.
"Min qabl" is an example of this rule.
"Tarmihim bi-hijarah" is the classic example of this rule.
"Lahum ma" is an example of this rule.
"Alam tara" is an example of this rule.
Izhar shafawi is strongest before these two letters, to avoid hiding.
Mim mushaddadah and nun mushaddadah carry this.
The ra' is read heavy when it has fathah or this.
The ra' with sukun after a kasrah is read this way, as in "fir'awn".
The ra' with sukun after kasrah but before a heavy letter is read heavy, as in this word.
The word "Allah" after "bismi" is read with this lam.
The madd tabi'i is also called this, the "original" madd.
A madd that lengthens more than two counts because of a hamzah or sukun is called this.
The two causes of madd far'i.
The madd 'iwad replaces tanwin fathah at a stop with this.
Stopping on a word ending in ta' marbutah, it is read as this.
Stopping on a word, its last vowel becomes this.
The lengthening when a madd letter is followed by hamzah in the same word.
The lengthening when a madd letter ends one word and hamzah begins the next.
The lengthening when a madd letter is followed by a sukun that stays in all cases.
The lengthening when the sukun comes only because you stop on the word.
The length of madd lazim in counts.
The lengths allowed in madd 'arid lil-sukun, in counts.
The lengthening for a madd letter that comes after a hamzah, as in "amanu".
The soft letters waw and ya' with sukun after a fathah.
The number of main areas of articulation (makharij) in Ibn al-Jazari's رحمة الله عليه scheme.
The number of specific makharij in Ibn al-Jazari's رحمة الله عليه scheme.
The empty space of the mouth and throat from which the madd letters come.
The nasal passage, makhraj of ghunnah.
The seven letters always read heavy.
The quality of the tongue rising toward the palate.
The quality of the tongue staying low.
The quality of a letter whose sound flows with breath.
The phrase that gathers the letters of hams.
The quality where the sound is held back strongly.
The phrase that gathers the letters of shiddah.
The letter with the quality of istitalah (stretching along the tongue's side).
Madd muttasil is lengthened in Hafs رحمة الله عليه by way of al-Shatibiyyah by this many counts.
Madd munfasil in Hafs رحمة الله عليه by way of al-Shatibiyyah.

The madd lin ('arid) as in "khawf" when stopping.
The four kinds of madd lazim.

"Al-taammah" in al-Nazi'at is an example of this madd lazim.
In "Alif Lam Mim", the "Mim" meeting the next mim with idgham is this kind.
The opening letter alif has this many counts.
The opening letters that take two counts are gathered in this phrase.

items.q: The makhraj of qaf.
items.a: Deepest part of the tongue with the soft palate

items.q: The makhraj of kaf.
items.a: Just below qaf, a little forward

items.q: The makhraj of jim, shin and ya'.
items.a: Middle of the tongue with the palate

items.q: The makhraj of dad.
items.a: Side(s) of the tongue with the upper molars

items.q: The makhraj of lam.
items.a: Edge of the tongue, front part, with the gums

items.q: The letters ta', dal and ta' (heavy) come from here.
items.a: Tip of the tongue with the roots of the upper front teeth

items.q: The letters za', dhal and tha' come from here.
items.a: Tip of the tongue with the edges of the upper front teeth

items.q: The letters sad, zay and sin come from here.
items.a: Tip of the tongue near the lower front teeth

items.q: The makhraj of fa'.
items.a: Inside of the lower lip with the edges of the upper front teeth

items.q: The ghunnah is strongest (most complete) in this case.
The quality of rakhawah (looseness) means the sound does this.
The opposite of hams (whispering).
The opposite of itbaq.
The opposite of idhlaq.
The quality of deviation (inhiraf) is in these two letters.
The quality of softness (lin) is in waw and ya' when they are this.
Ibn al-Jazari's رحمة الله عليه poem says "Whoever does not perfect the Qur'an is" this (paraphrased).
The heavy letters in order of strength begin with this kind.
items.a: Letters of itbaq (sad, dad, ta', za')

items.q: The alif follows the letter before it in heaviness or lightness; this is called this.
The "silent" letters at the end, like alif in "ana", are kept when stopping but dropped when this.
The kind of stop where the reciter stops on a word against the rule to show its ruling.
A stop the reader picks freely, without need, at a fitting place.
The quality of whistling found in sad, zay and sin.
The quality of spreading found in shin.
The quality of repetition (trilling) in ra', which the reciter keeps light.
The quality of covering (tongue sealed to the palate) in four letters.
The four letters of itbaq.
Idgham between two identical letters.
Idgham between two letters with the same makhraj but different qualities, as ta' into dal.
Idgham between two letters with close makharij, as lam into ra'.
The kind of idgham where the first letter vanishes fully.
The kind of idgham where some of the first letter's quality stays, as nun into waw with ghunnah.
The four words where nun sakinah meets waw or ya' in one word and stays clear, as in "dunya".
The stop at a point where the meaning is complete and does not join the next.
The stop that is complete in meaning but tied in meaning to what follows.
A stop that is not allowed because it breaks or spoils the meaning.
A short pause without breath, as in Hafs رحمة الله عليه at "'iwaja" in al-Kahf.
The number of required saktat in Hafs رحمة الله عليه by way of al-Shatibiyyah.
Stopping on a word to test or teach a student.
Stopping because breath runs out.
Restarting from a suitable point after a stop is called this.
The one word in Hafs رحمة الله عليه read with imalah (tilting the alif toward ya').
The four saktat of Hafs رحمة الله عليه: "'iwaja" (al-Kahf), "marqadina" (Yasin), "man raq" (al-Qiyamah) and this.
"Man raq" is in this surah.
"Bal ran" is in this surah.
"Marqadina" is in this surah.
In "nun wal-qalam" Hafs رحمة الله عليه reads the nun with this rule, via al-Shatibiyyah.
In "Ya Sin wal-Qur'an" Hafs رحمة الله عليه reads the nun of "sin" with this rule.
In "irkab ma'ana" (Hud), Hafs رحمة الله عليه reads the ba' with this rule.
In "yalhath dhalika" (al-A'raf), Hafs رحمة الله عليه reads this rule.
In "ahattu" (al-Naml), the heavy ta' merges into the light ta' but keeps this quality.
In "alam nakhluqkum" (al-Mursalat), the qaf merges into kaf in this way, the preferred way.
The word "da'f" in Surah al-Rum can be read by Hafs رحمة الله عليه with fathah or this vowel.
The word "al-musaytirun" (al-Tur) is read by Hafs رحمة الله عليه with sin or this letter.
The word "yabsutu" (al-Baqarah) is written with sad but read by Hafs رحمة الله عليه with this.
The word "bi-musaytir" (al-Ghashiyah) is read by Hafs رحمة الله عليه with this letter.
The word "salasila" (al-Insan) may be stopped on by Hafs رحمة الله عليه with an alif or this.
The word "ana" (I) is read short when joining; its alif is read only when this.
The word "lakinna huwa" (al-Kahf) has the alif of "lakinna" read only when this.
The term for a hamzah that is pronounced only at the start of speech.
The term for a hamzah always pronounced.
Hamzat al-wasl in a verb is read with dammah when the third letter has this.
Hamzat al-wasl in "al-" is always read with this vowel when starting.
Hamzat al-wasl in nouns like "ibn" and "ism" is read with this vowel when starting.
Two hamzahs where the second is hamzat al-wasl in "al-", as "a-al-dhakarayn", may be read with ibdal or this.
The ruling of the nun in "ta'manna" in Surah Yusuf is ishmam or this (ikhtilas).
Rawm means pronouncing part of a vowel at a stop, about this much.
Ishmam at a stop means rounding the lips after sukun without this.
Rawm is allowed only on these two vowels.
Ishmam at a stop is allowed only on this vowel.
The scholar who wrote the poem "al-Jazariyyah" also wrote this larger poem on the ten readings.
Ibn al-Jazari رحمة الله عليه died in this city.
The book that explains al-Jazariyyah, by Zakariyya al-Ansari رحمة الله عليه.
The book by Ibn al-Jazari رحمة الله عليه on the ten readings that his poem summarises.
The word in Surah Yusuf read with ishmam (lips rounded) in Hafs رحمة الله عليه.
The word in Fussilat read with tashil (softening) of the second hamzah in Hafs رحمة الله عليه.
The madd in the opening letters, as in "Lam" of Alif Lam Mim.
The phrase gathering the letters of the opening verses that take six counts.
The phrase gathering the opening letters read with two counts.
The opening letter that may take four or six counts.
The madd when a sukun follows a madd letter with shaddah inside a word, as in "al-dallin".
The madd for the ha' of the masculine pronoun between two vowels, as in "innahu huwa".
The silah madd when hamzah follows, lengthened like munfasil.
The word in al-Furqan where Hafs رحمة الله عليه lengthens the ha' though it follows a sukun.
Lengthening by four or five counts in munfasil, the usual length in Hafs رحمة الله عليه by way of al-Shatibiyyah.
The author of Tuhfat al-Atfal, Sulayman al-Jamzuri رحمة الله عليه, lived in this century AH.
The fluid quality of the letters fa', ra', mim, nun, lam and ba'.
The phrase gathering the letters of idhlaq.
The quality between shiddah and rakhawah found in lam, nun, 'ayn, mim and ra'.
The phrase gathering the letters of tawassut.
The ra' is read light when it has this vowel.
The teacher of Hafs in recitation, from whom his reading comes.

The larger way of Hafs رحمة الله عليه, with more options, comes through this poem.
The lengthening of munfasil by two counts (qasr) is allowed for Hafs رحمة الله عليه through this way.
The longest madd allowed for madd muttasil in some ways of Hafs رحمة الله عليه.

In Warsh's رحمة الله عليه reading, the ra' after a kasrah or ya' sakinah is often read this way.
In Warsh's رحمة الله عليه reading, the lam is read heavy after these three letters.

The number of the seven readers who read "maliki" in al-Fatihah without an alif.

The reader of Kufah who reads "al-sirat" with a sound between sad and zay (ishmam).
Qunbul رحمة الله عليه reads "al-sirat" with this letter.
The three readers added to the seven to make ten.
Ibn al-Jazari's رحمة الله عليه poem on the three extra readings.
The reader of Madinah among the three extra ones.
The reader of Basrah among the three extra ones.
Khalaf al-'Ashir was also a transmitter of this reader of the seven.
Ghunnah is a quality of nun and mim that has no this.
The number of qualities with opposites in al-Jazariyyah.
The number of qualities without opposites in al-Jazariyyah.
The letter that has the most "strong" qualities, said to be the strongest letter.
The letter considered the weakest, as it has the fewest strong qualities.
The famous reciter of Egypt known for the "mujawwad" style, d. 1409 AH / 1988 CE.
The Egyptian reciter known for the "murattal" recording of the whole Qur'an in several readings, d. 1401 AH / 1980 CE.
